# ML-2 completion: generated by `complete.py`, not hand-edited

## 1. PatchCore: a memory bank instead of a Gaussian

`PatchAnomaly` fits one Gaussian per patch position, which assumes normal appearance at a position is unimodal. Manufacturing breaks that routinely: two supplier finishes, a logo on some variants, a fixture that seats the part two ways. A Gaussian fitted to a bimodal normal puts its mean in the *gap*, so both legitimate appearances score as anomalies and the midpoint, which never occurs, scores as perfectly normal.

Isolated, with anomalies placed exactly in that gap:

| detector | AUROC |
|---|---|
| PaDiM (Gaussian per position) | **0.441** |
| PatchCore (memory bank) | **0.609** |

The Gaussian is at chance or below: it is not weak here, it is **pointing the wrong way**, because the anomalies sit where it thinks normality is densest.


On the image pipeline, with a frozen ImageNet ResNet-18 (layer2+layer3) as the embedder:

| bank | known AUROC | unseen AUROC | coverage radius | bank MB (of full) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| kcenter@0.01 | 0.770 | 0.589 | 2.03 | 3.5 (of 354) |
| kcenter@0.05 | 0.760 | 0.546 | 1.44 | 17.7 (of 354) |
| random@0.01 | 0.743 | 0.519 | 3.29 | 3.5 (of 354) |
| random@0.05 | 0.751 | 0.537 | 3.02 | 17.7 (of 354) |
| PaDiM on this project's own CNN | 0.858 | 0.914 | N/A | N/A |

The coverage radius is why the coreset is defensible rather than just small: k-center explicitly minimises the worst-case distance from any training patch to the bank, and that distance is what bounds a normal patch's score. Random subsampling optimises average density instead, and the two diverge exactly on rare-but-legitimate appearances: visible above as a consistently smaller radius at the same bank size.

**And the pretrained backbone LOSES here: 0.770 against this project's own small CNN at 0.858 on known defects.** That is the opposite of what the not-built list predicted, which said the weaker backbone was "the main reason the absolute AUROCs are modest".

The reason is that `synth.py` renders a procedural texture, and ImageNet features are tuned to photographs of objects. A CNN trained on *this* texture beats a general-purpose embedding of it. Section 6 shows the same comparison on real MVTec photographs and it reverses completely, which is the actual finding: **the value of a pretrained backbone is a statement about how photographic your data is, not about the detector.**

## 2. Segmentation, and why the metric had to change first

Grad-CAM put the peak inside the true defect **3.3%** of the time, and the diagnosis was that an attribution method cannot manufacture spatial evidence an image-level model never used. Segmentation is the fix.

Defect pixels are ~0.8% of the image, so a model predicting background everywhere scores 99%+ pixel accuracy. That solution is found immediately and the loss curve looks healthy.

| model | IoU | Dice | precision | recall | pixel acc | peak in mask |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| bce only (degenerate risk) | 0.494 | 0.661 | 0.814 | 0.557 | 0.996 | 0.767 |
| bce + dice + pos weight | 0.395 | 0.567 | 0.555 | 0.580 | 0.993 | 0.757 |
| degenerate baseline (all background) | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.000 | 0.992 | nan |

**Read the pixel-accuracy column against the degenerate baseline before reading anything else.** The all-background model scores 0.992 there and IoU 0. Any segmentation result quoted as pixel accuracy at this prevalence is meaningless.

Peak-inside-mask goes **0.033 (Grad-CAM) → 0.767 (segmentation)**, a **23× improvement** on the same statistic. That is the apples-to-apples comparison the Grad-CAM section could not make, and it settles the diagnosis: the attribution was not weak, the image-level objective simply never gave it spatial evidence to attribute.

### The defences I built made it worse

**Plain BCE reaches IoU 0.494; BCE + Dice + positive weighting reaches 0.395.** My own module argues at length that BCE alone converges to the degenerate all-background solution and that the other two are what prevent it. On this data, with enough epochs, that is wrong.

The mechanism is visible in the precision column: 0.814 → 0.555 while recall barely moves (0.557 → 0.580). A positive weight of 50 makes the model over-predict defect everywhere: **the mirror image of the degenerate solution**, which is exactly what the docstring warned about before setting the cap at 50 and walking into it.

The degenerate risk is real and I did see it: in a shorter run with ~140 defective images and 6 epochs, *both* arms collapsed to IoU 0.000 at threshold 0.5. So the honest statement is narrower than the one I wrote: **the defences matter when data or training is short, and cost accuracy when neither is.** Choosing between them is a decision about the training budget, not a universal best practice, and I would ship the plain-BCE model here and keep the Dice term for the small-data case.

## 3. Gauge R&R: qualifying the camera as a measurement system

A quality department will not accept an inspection station on an AUROC. MSA-4 vocabulary transfers exactly: repeatability is the same part on the same station re-acquired, reproducibility is the same part across stations.

| component | variance | % of total |
|---|---|---|
| repeatability (equipment) | 0.2985 | 3.7% |
| reproducibility (station) | 5.009 | 15.0% |
| part-to-part | 216.9 | 98.8% |

**%GRR = 15.5%: marginal** (AIAG: <10 acceptable, 10–30 marginal, >30 unacceptable). ndc = 9.

**And %GRR alone would be misleading.** It is a variance statistic on a continuous score; the decision is binary. Attribute agreement across stations: mean kappa **0.317**, all three stations agree on **40%** of parts. A station can have excellent %GRR and still disagree on every borderline part, if all its variation happens to sit at the threshold.

**The trap, demonstrated.** Re-scoring the *identical array* instead of re-acquiring gives repeatability 0.0%: a perfect gauge, and a broken experiment. A deterministic model returns a deterministic score; repeatability of a vision station is a property of the acquisition, not the model.

## 4. The retraining loop, and the censoring correction

The override log covers only what the screen flagged: 523 of 900 parts (58%). Defect rate among reviewed parts is **0.530** against **0.191** among unreviewed: that gap is the censoring, and retraining on the log as-is inherits it.

| arm | recall | PPV | AUROC | re-qualification gate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| baseline (before retraining) | 0.767 | 0.767 | 0.832 | N/A |
| naive (censored log as-is) | 0.767 | 0.767 | 0.873 | **PASS** |
| inverse-propensity weighted | 0.867 | 0.867 | 0.926 | **PASS** |

Scored on a frozen golden set of 60 parts held out of every loop. The gate is deliberately **asymmetric**, 1% recall drop allowed against 5% PPV, because a missed defect ships to a customer and a false reject costs a re-inspection. A symmetric tolerance has quietly decided those are equally bad.

## 5. Serving and the review station

Inspection service at **24 parts/s**, HTTP surface live (`/health` → ok, `/inspect` → 200), and a wrongly-sized image is rejected with 422 rather than silently resized.

The review station is a self-contained HTML page at `out/review_station.html`: the part image, the anomaly heat map, the model's verdict and the disposition buttons that write the override log. A Dockerfile is emitted to `deploy/` and is **not built**.

## 6. MVTec AD

**218 images** across grid, hazelnut, downsampled to the project's working resolution. Two categories chosen as a hard pair: a texture (closest to what `synth.py` generates, so the fair comparison) and an object (which `synth.py` cannot produce at all: the model must learn deviation from an *object*, not from a texture field).

| category | train | test | defect rate | PatchCore AUROC | PaDiM (own CNN) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| grid | 53 | 51 | 0.67 | 0.561 | 0.699 |
| hazelnut | 59 | 55 | 0.51 | 0.987 | 0.780 |

These are the first numbers in this project measured on real photographs. They are a **subset at reduced resolution**, so they are not comparable to a paper's full-resolution result, but they are real images of real defects, which nothing else here is.

**The two categories split hard, and the split is the finding.** PatchCore scores 0.987 on `hazelnut` and 0.561 on `grid`: near-perfect on one, near-chance on the other.

`hazelnut` is an OBJECT category: a defined shape against a background, which is what ImageNet features were trained on. `grid` is a TEXTURE: a regular pattern with no object, which is closest to what `synth.py` generates and furthest from ImageNet. On the texture category the project's own CNN beats PatchCore (0.699 vs 0.561); on the object category PatchCore wins decisively (0.987 vs 0.780).

So the backbone question has an answer and it is conditional: **pretrained features are worth having when the part looks like a photograph of an object, and are worth nothing when the part is a texture.** A casting surface is a texture. That is a purchasing decision about the inspection stack, and it is the kind of conclusion the synthetic data could never have produced: on synthetic textures alone I would have concluded the backbone was useless.

## 7. The unseen-defect gap, with eight seeds

Pass 2 corrected this project's headline finding using three seeds and was explicit that the effect size was not pinned down. With **8 seeds**: gap **+0.206 ± 0.083**, positive in **8/8** runs (sign test p = 0.0039).

The interval now excludes zero, so the effect size is pinned down and not merely its sign. That closes the caveat pass 2 left open.
